title: Networking: warm contacts, trade partners and local businesses
audience: Solo operators and team owners in any Titan Academy business who want introductions and referrals through people they already know, trade partners and local businesses.
learningOutcomes: List the warm contacts and local businesses that could send or receive work, and write one specific request for each group.
Draft a written referral arrangement with a complementary trade that covers referrals, complaints and any reward.
Introduce your business in under a minute at a local event or group, within that group's rules, and state the referral you want.

instruction.heading: Start with the people who already buy from you
instruction.body: Every business owner you pay for a service is a possible route to new work. Your accountant, mechanic, vet, physiotherapist, bookkeeper, dentist, real estate agent and the owners of the local shops you use all meet people who need what you offer. Write a list of these contacts, then tell each one what you do, what kind of client you want next, and what a suitable introduction would look like. Ask one direct question rather than handing over a long pitch: do you know anyone who needs this at the moment? Follow up once a quarter with a short update, because people remember the ones who keep them informed.

instruction.heading: Form written partnerships with complementary trades
instruction.body: Complementary trades serve the same customers without competing for the same job. Examples include a gardener and a pool technician, a cleaner and a carpet cleaner, a handyman and a locksmith, a dog walker and a pet sitter, or a personal trainer and a massage therapist. Before either party refers anyone, agree in writing what each does with a referral, how the handover works, who speaks to the customer first, how a complaint is handled if the partner's work goes wrong, and whether any reward is paid. Also agree what happens when a lead falls outside one partner's scope or licence. Put the agreement in a short document that both sides sign, and keep any reward at a level both sides can explain to a customer.

instruction.heading: Example: approaching a property or building business with a specific offer
instruction.body: A property or building business is one example of a business that can have recurring needs suited to home-service work. Property managers, real estate offices, strata managers and builders' site offices are typical examples. Examples of such needs include turnaround cleans between tenancies, gardening for common areas, minor repairs in vacant units, and clean-ups before inspections. The same approach applies to any business with a recurring need you can meet: arrive with one written offer for that need, a clear description of how you price it, and two or three questions about what the current supplier misses. Book the meeting in advance, follow the reception and site rules, and do not attend a site where you have not been invited. Leave a short document with your insurance details, licence details and contact details, and note the agreed next step before you leave.

instruction.heading: Use business groups and events with a prepared introduction
instruction.body: Local business groups, trade associations, council-run business sessions and networking events can introduce you to other owners. Some councils keep a directory of local business networks, from informal dinner groups to formal referral organisations that trade referrals between members. Wyndham City Council in Victoria is one example, so check the directory for your own council. Before you attend, read the group's rules on visitors and on pitching. Prepare an introduction of about thirty seconds that says who you help, what problem you solve and what kind of introduction you would welcome. Listen more than you speak, ask two or three questions about the other person's business, and offer one practical tip that costs them nothing. If a group forbids pitching, follow that rule even if you think your service would help the room. Record who you met and what each person offered, and follow up within two working days.

instruction.heading: Be present at community events where the rules allow it
instruction.body: School fairs, sports club days, community markets and neighbourhood events let people in your area see your name and your work. Before you book a stall or a sponsorship, check the organiser's rules on trading and promotion, and any fees or insurance the organiser requires. Keep your table focused on the service and one practical tip, such as a seasonal checklist, with a simple quote-request sheet beside it. Collect contact details only with the person's agreement, and tell them what you will do with those details. Count the enquiries that became paid work so you can decide whether returning next season is worth the cost.

procedure: List your warm contacts, and write one specific request for each group.
Choose two complementary trades and draft a referral agreement covering referrals, complaints and any reward.
Identify two businesses with a recurring need you can meet, such as a property or building business, and prepare one written offer.
Check the rules of one business group or event before you attend or book.
Prepare and rehearse a thirty-second introduction, then use it within the group's rules.
Record every contact and follow up within two working days.
Review at the end of the quarter which contacts and events produced paid work.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner and a gardener serve the same group of strata buildings. The gardener's committee contact asks whether anyone can clean the building entrances every week.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the cleaner check and agree before she takes the referral?
workedExamples.reasoning: She checks the scope of the entrance work, how she prices it, the insurance she holds for the work, and whether the work needs any licence or training in her state or territory. She and the gardener agree in writing who speaks to the committee first, how a complaint is handled if the cleaning goes wrong, and what reward, if any, the gardener receives. She does not accept the job until the scope and the terms are written down and both parties have agreed to them.

equipmentAndPpe: Warm-contact list with requests and follow-up dates
Draft referral agreement template for a partner trade
One-page business summary with insurance and licence details
Event rules and booking confirmation for any stall or sponsorship
No PPE is needed for meetings; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Asking a warm contact to buy on the spot, or sending a long pitch in place of a question.
commonErrors.prevention: Explain what you do and the kind of client you want, then ask one direct question.

commonErrors.error: Agreeing a referral with a trade without writing down the terms.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the referral, complaint and reward terms, and have both parties sign before the first referral.

commonErrors.error: Pitching in a group or at an event that forbids it.
commonErrors.prevention: Read the rules before attending or booking, and follow them on the day.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a referral for work that falls outside your licence or insurance.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance for each referred job before you accept it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not pitch at a group, event or venue that forbids it. Read the rules before attending or booking, and follow them on the day.

A referral does not transfer a licence, insurance or authority. Work that needs a licence, such as electrical, gas or other restricted work, must be done by someone licensed for it in the state or territory where the work is done. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule in each one you work in. This lesson does not grant any licence.
Referral rewards and partner payments may carry tax, contract and insurance implications. Check the arrangement with an adviser before you start.

If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business, contact details collected at events or meetings are personal information, and they should be used only for the purpose the person agreed to. The OAIC's small business guidance (summary read 2026-11-03) says a small business with annual turnover of $3 million or less is generally exempt, but some small businesses are covered regardless, so check whether the Act applies to you. Even where it does not, use the details only for the purpose the person agreed to.

qualityStandard: Every warm contact has a specific request and a follow-up date.
Every referral arrangement is written, signed by both parties and covers referrals, complaints and any reward.
No referral is accepted for work outside the licence and insurance held by the business that accepts it.
documentationEvidence: Warm-contact list with the request made, the date and the follow-up date.
Signed or agreed referral arrangement with a partner trade.
Event or group attendance record with the rules checked and the follow-ups made.
summary: Your existing business contacts are a practical route to introductions, so ask them one clear question.
Put every referral arrangement in writing before the first referral is made.
Follow the rules of each group or event, and measure which contacts produced paid work.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the most useful first step with someone on your warm contact list?
options: Ask them to buy your service on the spot and offer a special price today only if they book this week
Explain what your business does and the kind of client you want, then ask whether they know anyone who needs it
Send them a full price list without any conversation and ask them to reply by Friday with a yes or no

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a written partnership with another trade cover?
options: Only the logos each business will use and the colours
The number of followers each business has today
Referral handling, complaint handling and any reward

knowledgeChecks.question: A business group forbids pitching at its meetings. What should you do?
options: Follow the rule and do not pitch; take part only as the group allows
Pitch briefly, because your service would help the room
Hand out cards to the members privately, since the rule is for meetings
